1:
The psalm opens in petition. Adam Clarke notes that such frequency shows David’s earnestness: if God did not hear he could succeed nowhere else, and so he keeps knocking at the gate of mercy. C.H. Spurgeon observes that the saints run to the mercy-seat as chickens to the hen in danger, but that the bare act of prayer never satisfies them: they crave an audience with heaven and an answer from the throne. The plea that God not hide himself he explains from a man who sees a neighbour in distress and passes by, and finds its darkest instance in the cross. Matthew Henry takes the phrase two ways, of one unconcerned and of one angry at the prayer itself; if we lay our case open sincerely, he answers, we may hope God will not hide his favours.

What lies behind the trouble they answer differently. Matthew Henry hears Absalom’s party, stirring the people up against David. John Calvin concludes from the opening language that the distress was heavy, since no ordinary amount could overwhelm a saint of such courage, and refers the threatenings to Saul; he rejects a rendering that makes David boast of his fortitude, against a context anxious to convey wretchedness. John Gill names Absalom on the authority of Arama, or Ahithophel, who gave out that he would smite the king only, and carries the complaint forward to the Pharisees reproaching Christ. Adam Clarke reads it as the method of insurrection: to give a colourable pretence to rebellion they charge the king with horrible crimes, clamour against the sovereign being always the watchword. John Wesley sums the clauses as clamours, threats and slanders, with many crimes laid to his charge.

The mourning itself draws close attention to the words. Charles Ellicott observes that the verb rendered I mourn occurs in this form in only three other passages, always with the idea of restlessness — a Bedouin’s roving life in Genesis 27:40, moral restlessness, political instability — so that it may point either to the bodily restlessness that serves as an outlet of grief or to the distracted mind itself; and he renders the next clause and must roar, the verb expressing a compulsion to give vent in groans. For the next image he prefers roll mischief to cast iniquity, the figure drawn from rolling stones on an enemy from a height. Keil and Delitzsch work the same ground from the Hebrew side, noting that the noun means both a shrub and reflection or care, and that the verb used elsewhere of a roving life here means to be inwardly uneasy. They also gloss the plea about hiding: since what is in question is audible rather than visible, veil not thyself means veil not thine ear, as in Lamentations 3:56 — which God does designedly when the right state of heart has left the one praying. Adam Clarke hears in the Hebrew a strong guttural sound expressive of the natural accents of sorrow, and renders the clause I am in a tumult.

Whether such noise is a good sign they differ. Matthew Henry defends it: great griefs are sometimes noisy and are in some measure lessened by it, while those that are stifled increase. C.H. Spurgeon agrees that the psalmist gives a loose to his sorrows and lets his mind rehearse her griefs in whatever language suggests itself, and notes that the same request is made three times — a mark of deep and bitter earnest. Augustine of Hippo looks past the trouble to the superscription. The end named there is Christ, the end of the law; and there are two kinds of end, the end that consumes, as food is ended in eating, and the end that perfects, as a garment is ended in weaving. When you hear at the end in the psalms, let the thought be not of consuming but of consummation.
4:
The terror is described before it is explained. Charles Ellicott renders the opening verb writhes with pain, and takes terrors of death to mean terrors caused by death, a horror of it. John Calvin notes the same word, which usually means the pains a woman feels in travail, and draws from it that these are no ordinary sufferings: the man who uses them was no soft person but one who had given indubitable proofs of constancy. Adam Clarke follows the sequence and admires it — distress, mourning, sobs and sighs, a wounded heart, the expectation of death, then fear, then tremor, ending in deep apprehension of inevitable ruin — and adds that no man ever described a wounded heart like David. He glosses the middle clause plainly: I am in hourly expectation of massacre. John Gill refers the pain to the civil war in the kingdom, and to Christ in the garden, sorrowful unto death.

Whether such collapse is a fault John Calvin answers directly: the passage teaches that the fortitude of the greatest servants of God fails them in the hour of severe trial. We are all good soldiers so long as things go well, but brought to close combat our weakness is soon apparent, and Satan avails himself of it, suggesting that God has withdrawn the supports of his Spirit. David struggles with inward fears as well as outward calamities, on the very eve of sinking unless divine grace interpose.

The wish for wings turns the comment to natural history. Charles Ellicott identifies the bird as the rock pigeon, which nests in lofty cliffs and ravines far from the neighbourhood of man, comparing Song of Solomon 2:14; and where the versions have be at rest, he judges the parallelism to require the more literal dwell or abide. John Gill thinks the creature chosen because the enemies were like the ravenous hawk and he the harmless trembling dove, and for its swiftness; Aben Ezra’s reason he reports instead, that the dove is sociable with men, who send letters by them for quick despatch. Adam Clarke supposes David so hemmed in that he could see no escape unless he had wings, and suggests that doves passing before his eyes prompted the figure.

John Calvin gathers the whole bird into the image: its defencelessness, its danger from birds of prey, and the rapidity with which, pursued by the hawk, it flees to deserts and rocks. He finds the same allusion at Jeremiah 48:28, quotes Sophocles wishing he could cleave the ethereal clouds with the whirlwind flight of a dove, and passes on Kimshi’s reason for preferring the dove: other birds weary and must alight to recruit their strength, and so are taken, but the dove when fatigued rests one wing and flies with the other, escaping the swiftest pursuers.

The flight is given both a history and a use. John Gill notes that David did wander far off when he fled from Absalom, and that gracious souls desire the like — not the wilderness of the people but a solitude clear of wicked company; he extends it to the primitive church fleeing into the wilderness of the Gentiles, and reads the windy storm and tempest as an invading army, and as the wrath the sinner escapes by fleeing to Christ. Adam Clarke keeps to the history — David did escape, though his enemies were near enough to throw stones at him, and got beyond Jordan — and identifies the sweeping wind and tempest as Absalom, his party and the mutinous people. He then sets beside the psalm a passage from Seneca’s Octavia, in Latin with an English verse translation by his son: the speaker, having no words to bewail her woes, wishes for Philomel’s wings, to be borne far from mankind and there, in a grove of sad silence, to pour her moan from a slender spray.
9:
The psalm turns from flight to imprecation. Charles Ellicott notes that the opening verb means swallow up, that the Greek renders it forcibly as drown in the sea, and that the object has to be supplied; the sudden change from plaintive sadness to violent invective is a marked feature of the poem, and though some suspect a transposition, such transitions are not uncommon in lyric poetry. John Gill takes the verb historically, as Pharaoh was swallowed up in the Red Sea and Korah in the earth, and carries it to the last enemy, death. John Calvin reports a conjecture of Hare and Green that the first verb was not destroy but divide, giving an elegant repetition of the kind Scripture elsewhere affords.

The second clause all refer to Babel. John Wesley glosses it destroy them by dividing — their speech as at Genesis 11:9, their votes and counsels. Charles Ellicott renders it cause division in their councils. John Calvin finds the allusion to Babel plain and generalises it: God still weakens the enemies of the church by splitting them into factions through mutual animosities. Adam Clarke, John Wesley and C.H. Spurgeon all note that the prayer was granted in fact: Hushai and Ahithophel gave opposite counsel, Absalom followed Hushai, and Ahithophel, knowing what it would bring, went and hanged himself. C.H. Spurgeon presses the point into an aphorism — revolution devours its own children — and observes that the one went to be hanged with a rope and the other without one.

The picture of the city draws the fullest comment. Matthew Henry reads it as the grief of a king whose capital has turned: Jerusalem strangely fell in with Absalom and fell off from David, so that he had none there but his own guards to trust, and saw with his own eyes nothing but violence and strife. All the arts the rebels used to fortify the place were made up of violence and strife, with no remains of honesty or love among them, and in the heart of the city were mischief and injury and mutual wrong. Wickedness, he says, was legalised.

What patrols the walls they divide over. Charles Ellicott holds it in keeping with Hebrew style to suppose mischief and strife personified, as the ancient versions do, not inhabiting the city but prowling about its walls, and compares Virgil’s line on grief and terror everywhere and death in a thousand shapes. John Wesley takes the same view, violence and strife encompassing the city like a garrison. John Gill makes the irony explicit: men of violence and contention are its only watchmen, and a city must be sadly guarded that has no better watch. Adam Clarke keeps to the men, and says the two verses exhibit any city at the beginning of an insurrection, its leaders plotting continually and sowing dissension by misrepresentation, calumny and lies.

Of the last verse John Gill says only that wickedness has here filled up its measure. Charles Ellicott corrects two words: deceit is rather oppression, and streets rather squares, the open space at an Oriental city’s gate where public business was done — a miserable picture of misgovernment, since in the very seat of justice there is nothing but oppression and guile. John Wesley takes the same word for the places of public commerce. John Calvin explains why the catalogue runs so long: the psalmist insists on his adversaries’ wickedness to encourage himself in prayer, since in proportion as men grow rampant in sin may the divine judgments be expected. He adds a caution about the complaint itself — had David indulged longer in that strain he might have sanctioned the folly of those who do themselves more harm than good by so barren a species of comfort — allowing that exclamations not altogether justifiable will escape a saint at prayer, though he soon recalls himself to believing supplication.
12:
C.H. Spurgeon observes that the psalmist described his own poem when he said he would give loose to his thoughts, wandering from one point of sorrow to another like a man in a maze; here his mind turns from the turbulent city to the false-hearted councillor. The complaint he states as a rule: none are such enemies as false friends. Reproaches from those once intimate with us cut to the quick, since they know where we are most sensitive, and the slanders of an avowed antagonist, lacking ingratitude, are less hard to bear. We can bear from Shimei what we cannot endure from Ahithophel; an open foe can be hidden from, treachery cannot.

John Calvin makes the same point by a correction. Those mistake the sense who take the verb to mean that David could have borne an open enemy’s reproach; what he says is that he could have parried it, as one turns aside a blow. Against a known foe we are on our watch, but the unsuspected stroke of a friend takes us by surprise; the sum of the complaint is a treachery so secret that self-defence was impossible. Charles Ellicott supplies the ellipse from the imprecation above and renders the second half then, or else, I might bear it.

Who the traitor was is the chief dispute. Adam Clarke thinks Ahithophel meant throughout, since he was at the bottom of the conspiracy from the beginning and probably first moved the vain mind of Absalom. John Wesley agrees that all of it fits Ahithophel. John Gill reports the Targum and Talmud for the same man, though he cites Arama for Absalom, and takes the verses mystically of Judas — not a sworn enemy of Christ but one of his apostles. John Calvin dissents from the whole field: he does not imagine it was Ahithophel, since the psalm does not appear to him to have been written upon Absalom’s persecution at all. Whether it was some traitor in Keilah is impossible to determine; the least improbable conjecture is a great man at court whose intimacy with David was well known — perhaps more than one, courtiers who had sacrificed friendship to a desire of rising.

The friend himself is described closely. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase a man of my own standing. The noun is the word used at Exodus 40:23 of the row of loaves that made the shewbread, its cognate verb meaning to arrange; here it may denote rank, but more probably means man of my assessment, of like importance in society. The Greek and Latin versions have of one soul with me, Symmachus of like disposition — a sense implied though not expressed in the Hebrew. For the next word he resists the old versions: the Hebrew denotes the head of a tribe, but that seems excluded by the description just given, and he would render companion. John Wesley reaches the same plainly — equal not in power but in reputation, for wisdom and influence — and takes guide of one whose counsel David constantly followed.

The last verse turns on what the two shared. John Gill takes the sweet counsel as civil rather than religious, since in religious matters the testimonies of the Lord were David’s counsellors; hearty counsel, he says, is a branch of friendship and greatly sweetens it. Applied to Christ and Judas it denotes the delight one had in communicating and the other in receiving a notional knowledge of the gospel; and he defends this by asking why, if hearers may hear the word gladly as Herod did, preachers devoid of grace may not preach it speculatively with some pleasure. Charles Ellicott reads the closing clause of joining the great public processions to the temple, and notes that the word rendered company appears elsewhere as insurrection — so the intimacy of these former friends was public as well as private.
15:
The verse is the harshest in the psalm, and the question is whether such a prayer may be prayed. John Calvin answers carefully. The curse falls on the faction, not the nation, and only on those who took a prominent part in the persecution; in uttering it David was not influenced by bad feeling but must be understood as speaking in God’s cause and not his own, under the immediate guidance of his Spirit. It was no wish let fall in resentment or reckless zeal, and gives no warrant to launch maledictions on every trivial provocation: the spirit of revenge differs widely from the holy and regulated fervour with which David prays for God’s judgment against men already doomed.

C.H. Spurgeon concedes more and defends it differently. Not thus would Jesus pray; but the rough soldier David so poured out the anguish of his spirit under a treachery seldom equalled and altogether unprovoked, and a soldier desires the overthrow of his foes, since for that end he fights. Viewed as law and justice David was right, waging a just defensive war; the words should be read as a warrior’s imprecation, and traitors like these deserve to die, being a pest to the commonwealth. Yet he offers an alternative that empties the verse of imprecation: there is no need to read it as a curse at all, for it may as well be a confident expectation or prophecy — God would, he was sure, cast them out of the land of the living.

The opening verb is disputed. Charles Ellicott reports that the written text gives desolations upon them, and calls the verse another outburst of overmastering feeling. John Gill offers let him exact upon them, as a creditor demanding of a debtor the debt of punishment for sin, or let him come upon them unawares, so that they die not a natural but a violent death. John Calvin reports Horsley’s objection: the image is not sufficiently expressed by the English word, and though the translators may have meant the seizure of a debtor, that is a kindred image rather than the same, the precise one being the exaction of payment, not the seizure of the person. Horsley renders it let death exalt his claim upon them; Calvin prefers the received version. Adam Clarke arrives at much the same: death shall exact upon them, they shall descend alive into sheol.

The second clause they take of a sudden grave. Charles Ellicott glosses quick as alive, perhaps recalling the fate of Korah, and drops the final conjunction, rendering in their dwellings, in their very midst. John Calvin also hears the punishment of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, but thinks the point of praying for sudden ruin lies in the proud persuasion these men cherished in prosperity that they would escape the stroke of death. John Wesley reads a cutting off by sudden and violent death, and renders the last words from the Hebrew as in their inwards — wickedness deeply rooted in their hearts.

Who is meant they set out from history. John Gill names Ahithophel and his accomplices, and Judas and the men with him, noting that the Targum mentions Doeg. John Wesley widens it to all who pretend to religion and have manifestly apostatised from the profession and the practice of it. Adam Clarke treats the verse as a prediction of the destruction that fell on the ringleaders, and finds it fulfilled: Ahithophel, his counsel rejected, hanged himself; Absalom fleeing was caught by the hair in a tree under which his mule had passed, and being found so by Joab was despatched with three darts; twenty thousand rebels were slain, and the wood devoured more people that day than the sword, as 2 Samuel 18:8 reports. C.H. Spurgeon tells the same story briefly: Ahithophel and Judas both soon ended their own lives, and Absalom was hanged in the oak.
16:
The psalm turns here, and deliberately. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as a refusal: the psalmist would not meet plots with counterplots nor imitate their incessant violence, but in direct opposition to their godless behaviour would resort continually to his God. The covenant name, he adds, is the pledge of the covenant promise. Matthew Henry hears the same defiance: let them take what course they please to secure themselves, and let violence and strife be their guards, prayer shall be mine. He grounds the confidence on Romans 10:13, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord in a right manner shall be saved.

John Calvin reads the verbs as future, since the psalmist is not referring to something already done but exciting himself to prayer and hope. Though he stood on the brink of destruction with no apparent escape, he declares his resolution to continue praying. Adam Clarke agrees that he foresaw his deliverance: the Lord shall save me, or as the Targum has it, the Word of the Lord shall redeem me. John Gill insists on the object — not a creature, not idols and images, not angels or saints departed, but God, who is able to save.

The resolution is made both fervent and frequent. Matthew Henry notes that the earlier word signifies to meditate: David will speak with his own heart and let the prayer come thence. We pray aright when we think first and then pray over our thoughts, prayer being the lifting up of the heart to God; having meditated he will cry aloud, the fervour of his spirit expressed and yet more excited by the earnestness of his voice. C.H. Spurgeon qualifies the loudness: some cry aloud who never say a word, and it is the bell of the heart that rings loudest in heaven. On frequency he is emphatic: often, but none too often, since great need calls for frequent devotion. To begin, continue and end the day with God is supreme wisdom, and where time has set a boundary let us set an altar-stone; the psalmist means he will always pray, tracking the sun with his petitions.

Why these three hours is answered from the temple. John Calvin infers that they must have been the stated hours among the godly of that period, since the daily morning and evening sacrifices taught the people to pray privately at home, and at noon additional sacrifices were offered. He then draws the rule: because we are naturally indisposed to the duty there is danger of omitting it altogether unless we restrict ourselves to a fixed order, God having had respect in appointing hours to the infirmity of our nature. Sacrifices have ceased in the church; the indisposition has not. John Gill supplies the Jewish detail, the hours being said to have been fixed by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: evening prayer answered the evening sacrifice at the ninth hour, when Peter and John went up to the temple; morning prayer the daily sacrifice at the third hour, when the apostles met at Pentecost; and noon fell at the sixth, when Peter went up to the housetop.

Adam Clarke calls it the custom of the pious Hebrews, citing Daniel 6:10, and explains the order: the Hebrews began their day in the evening, and hence David mentions the evening first. The rabbins, he reports, say men should pray three times daily because the day changes three times, and the practice was kept in the primitive church. He then gives what he calls the curious turn of the Old Psalter, which makes each hour commemorate a stage of the Lord’s work: at even his praise is told for the time Christ was on the cross, at morn for his rising from the dead, and at midday he hears the voice of one sitting at his Father’s right hand, whither he ascended at midday.
18:
The deliverance is spoken of as past, and the tense is the first difficulty. John Calvin observes that those who read the preceding verses as perfect take David to be proving his prayers answered from the deliverance granted; but the other reading holds. He may have been so confident of deliverance that he speaks as if it were done, or may be inserting meditations made at different times, it being common, when prayers are mentioned, to subjoin the event. John Wesley says the same in a line: he speaks of a future deliverance as done, because of the certainty of it. John Gill takes the clause of past battles — God had brought him safe from many a fight that seemed at first to go against him, and given him rest before the present trouble came — and calls the inference the reasoning of faith.

The clause about the many divides them. John Calvin allows a double meaning. Some understand enemies, David being beset by adversaries and commending God’s goodness in his deliverance; others refer it to the angels, encamped round about those that fear the Lord, as at Psalm 34:7, taking the Hebrew prefix as merely expletive. John Wesley settles on the second: there were more with me than against me, even the holy angels whom God employed to defend and deliver me. Adam Clarke offers the Targum instead, that in many afflictions his Word was my support. Charles Ellicott will not settle it: the clause is intelligible only if the word fighting is inserted, giving many fighting with me, that is, against me — and the text, he says, seems corrupt. He prefers the Greek of the previous clause, from those drawing near to me, a divergence John Gill also reports.

The next verse is read two ways. John Gill takes God shall hear and afflict them of the psalmist’s imprecation granted, or renders it hear and answer them, God answering their blasphemies by terrible things. John Calvin agrees: the verb might mean to testify, so that God rises as a witness, but the syntax will scarcely admit it, and having said God would hear him David adds that he would answer by avenging his cause. On the title that follows, he that abideth of old, Calvin makes the pastoral point: much of the impatience into which we are hurried arises from not elevating our thoughts to the eternity of God, and nothing is more unreasonable than that mortals who pass like a shadow should measure him by their feeble apprehensions, casting him from his eternal throne into a changing world.

What the changes are is the last question. Adam Clarke takes them as reverses: Absalom and Ahithophel carried all before them at first, and suffering no reversal they feared not God. Most who have few afflictions, he adds, have but little religion, becoming sufficient to themselves and calling not upon God. John Wesley agrees: they meet no crosses, and their success makes them go on securely, without dread of God’s judgments. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same by the word itself, used elsewhere of a change of clothes, and here, with the Targum, of a change of mind; the plural means every such change is far from them, and the relative clause grounds their fate in their character, since they persevere in godlessness without regard to anyone.

Charles Ellicott turns the verse inside out, rendering it God shall hear and afflict them, he abideth of old, one in whom are no changes, and yet they fear not God — so the changelessness belongs to God, not to the wicked, and he compares James 1:17 on the Father with whom is no variableness. The received rendering, he says, does not suit the context; the word means variableness generally, used of troops relieving guard at Job 14:14; and the Selah must go as plainly out of place.
20:
The psalm returns to the traitor, and the question is whether one man is meant or several. John Calvin notes that the last verse speaks in the plural, but thinks it probable that here the writer addresses the leader and head of the conspiracy. Charles Ellicott agrees that the individual most prominent in the traitorous crew is singled out again. Adam Clarke makes it a further description of Ahithophel, who had agreed to serve David for his own emolument, but while receiving the king’s pay was endeavouring to subvert the kingdom and destroy the life of his sovereign. John Gill reads the verse of the cruelty, perfidy and hypocrisy of the false friend. John Wesley alone reads the singular as a plural, of the persons last mentioned.

What the breach was they set out alike. John Calvin accuses the man of waging war in the midst of peace: he had suffered no provocation and had not announced openly his intention to give battle, but commenced the attack unexpectedly and with treachery. C.H. Spurgeon says the same with more heat: he smites those to whom he had given the hand of friendship and is perfidious to men who dwell at ease on his friendly professions, profaning the most solemn league. Charles Ellicott supplies a literal sense for the verb: he perforated. In a note on the Creed, referring to Colossians 2:14, Bishop Pearson observed that one mode of cancelling a bond was to drive a nail through it — so breaking a covenant is here the piercing of the document.

The smooth words of the next verse draw the fullest comment. John Calvin takes the contrast as the whole point: to appearance the words were soft and agreeable, but they covered a hidden virulence which wounded like a sword. In the figurative language of the East, he notes, injurious words are often compared to swords, as at Proverbs 12:18; the figure is common in our own language too, in Hamlet’s I will speak daggers to her. He adds the proverb that deceivers carry on their lips poison besmeared with honey, and recalls the fair promises Saul addressed to David to entrap him — it being one special trial of the Lord’s people to be exposed to such attempts.

C.H. Spurgeon presses the same images harder. The traitor lauded and larded the man he hoped to devour; beware of a man with too much honey on his tongue, for a trap is to be suspected where the bait is so tempting, and oily words are most plentiful where truth is scarcest. He brought forth butter in a lordly dish, but had a tent-pin ready for his guest’s temples; when heart and lip differ so widely the man is a monster. His words were as yielding as the best juice of the olive — yet rapiers unsheathed.

Adam Clarke calls the man a complete courtier and designing hypocrite, and finds the verse a literal description of Absalom’s conduct at 2 Samuel 15:2: he waited at the gate, questioned those who came for justice, hinted broadly that the king was negligent and had provided no effective magistracy, and added that if he were made judge justice should be done to all; he bowed to the people and kissed them, and stole the hearts of the men of Israel. John Gill hears the words of Ahithophel in counsel with David, and behind them those of Judas at the kiss. Charles Ellicott, alone of them, doubts the text: the ancient versions and the grammatical anomalies point to a corruption, and he would read smoother than butter is his face, the substitution of face for mouth being suggested by the Greek, though that version has wandered far even from the amended text. The comparison of the tongue to a sword, he grants, is frequent; that of the words themselves less usual, but apt.
22:
The word rendered burden is peculiar to this passage. Charles Ellicott says it probably means gift, and hence lot or condition, though the Talmud uses it for burden and the Greek by rendering care prepared the way for the consolation of 1 Peter 5:7. John Calvin presses further: the verb behind the noun means to give, so that by the rules of grammar the phrase should be what is given thee, or as the Chaldee has it what thou hopest to receive. Most interpreters read burden, he observes, but assign no reason; the verb never denotes it, and they seem driven to invent the meaning by the harshness of the stricter translation. The sentiment is pious — there is no other way of relieving anxious souls than reposing on providence — but he finds no example of the usage.

John Gill takes the same reading and turns it to account: cast thy gift upon the Lord means what he has given in providence and grace, and also what he gives in the way of trial, the cross — a gift as the cup Christ drank was said to be given him by his Father. The words are either the Holy Ghost’s to David, according to Jarchi, or David’s to his own soul. John Wesley agrees, and takes the burden plainly as all thy crosses and cares and fears, laid on the Almighty by faith and prayer.

Adam Clarke reads it the same way: whatever cares oppress thee, lay them on him, for he shall bear both thee and thy burden; while a man is righteous and trusts in God he is as safe as if he were in heaven. C.H. Spurgeon holds both senses together: what thy God lays upon thee, lay thou upon the Lord — his wisdom casts it on thee, thy wisdom casts it back on him. The righteous may move like boughs in a tempest but never like a tree torn up by the roots: he stands firm who stands in God.

The last verse turns to the other end, and the difficulty is whether it is true. John Calvin raises the objection himself — does the claim that bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days consist with what we observe? — and answers that it applies not to common murderers but to tyrants, who consign their fellow creatures to slaughter for the gratification of their passions. He notes too that the Chaldee explains the pit as the deep Gehenna, and that David means a destruction not temporary but everlasting: the righteous may sink into many a pit of calamity and rise again, but their enemies’ ruin is deadly. Adam Clarke quotes the same Chaldee, which he calls emphatic, and reconciles the verse with providence differently: there is an appointed time beyond which a man cannot pass, yet he may so live as to provoke God to cut him off before half of it. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as irony: they were in heart the murderers of others and became in reality self-murderers, virtue lengthening life as vice shortens it.

John Wesley reads the closing confidence as patience, quietly waiting for deliverance; C.H. Spurgeon calls it a wise practical conclusion, the Lord being all that faith can need. John Gill names the men brought down as Ahithophel and his accomplices, and behind them Judas. Adam Clarke refuses that reading. The fathers in general, he says, apply the principal passages of this psalm to our Lord’s sufferings, the treason of Judas and the wickedness of the Jews, but these do not appear to him fairly deducible from the text. The psalm refers plainly enough to Absalom’s rebellion: the consternation of the earlier verses describes the king fleeing Jerusalem and going up the mount of Olives weeping, and the iniquity cast upon him answers to his son’s artful complaints and to Shimei’s reproach.
